Q8 is written in D-operator notation in the source; solved via the characteristic polynomial. Q21: the master says n>=1; the recurrence also holds for n=0.

qs.q: If $y(x)$ is the solution of the initial value problem $e^{y}\,dx-e^{-x}\,dy=0,\ y(0)=0$, then $y(x)=$
hints: The equation can be written with all $x$ terms on one side and all $y$ terms on the other, so it is separable.
Move $e^{-x}\,dy$ to the right side, then divide so that $dx$ goes with $x$ terms and $dy$ with $y$ terms, and integrate both sides.
For $f(y)\,dy=g(x)\,dx$ integrate both sides and fix the constant with the initial condition; then solve for $y$ using $\ln$ as the inverse of the exponential.

qs.q: The solution of the linear differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}-y=x^{2}\sin x$ is given by
hints: This is a first-order linear equation in $y$.
Divide by $x$ to get the standard form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$, then find the integrating factor.
$\rho=e^{\int P\,dx}$ and $(\rho y)'=\rho Q$.
steps: Standard form: $y'-\dfrac1x y=x\sin x$, so $\rho=e^{-\int dx/x}=\dfrac1x$ (for $x>0$).

qs.q: The solution of the exact differential equation $(2xy^{2}-3)\,dx+(2x^{2}y+4)\,dy=0$ is given by
hints: The problem states the equation is exact, so look for a potential function $F(x,y)$.
Integrate $M=2xy^2-3$ with respect to $x$, adding an unknown function $g(y)$, then match $F_y$ with $N$.
If $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ is exact then $F_x=M$, $F_y=N$, and the solution is $F(x,y)=c$.

qs.q: The solution of the homogeneous differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y-x}{y+x}$ is given by
hints: The right side is unchanged if $x,y$ are replaced by $sx,sy$, so the equation is homogeneous.
Divide the numerator and denominator by $x$ and substitute $v=y/x$.
With $y=vx$, $y'=v+xv'$ and the equation becomes separable; useful integrals: $\int\frac{dv}{1+v^2}=\tan^{-1}v$ and $\int\frac{2v\,dv}{1+v^2}=\ln(1+v^2)$.
Writing a vector as a linear combination leads to a linear system for $a,b,c$.
Equate components of $t=au+bv+cw$ to get three equations and solve them (Gaussian elimination or substitution).
Two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are equal exactly when all three components are equal.
steps: From the second, $c=7-2a$. The first gives $-a+3b=-5$; the third gives $-2a+b=-5$, so $b=2a-5$.

qs.q: The rank of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-3&0&-5\\-1&4&1&7\\2&1&7&4\\2&-2&4&-2\end{bmatrix}$ is equal to
hints: The rank is the number of nonzero rows after row reduction.
Use the first row to clear the entries below the first pivot and see what remains.
The rank of a matrix equals the number of pivots (nonzero rows) in its row echelon form.
steps: Only the rows $(1,-3,0,-5)$ and $(0,1,1,2)$ remain, so the rank is $2$.
qs.brief: Row reduce: rows 3 and 4 become zero, leaving 2 pivots, so rank $=2$.

qs.q: A basis for the subspace $W=\{(x,y,z):x-2y+5z=0\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ consist of
hints: $W$ is the solution set of one homogeneous equation, so find its free variables.
Solve for $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z$, write the general vector, and split it into one vector per free variable.

A basis of the solution space of a homogeneous system has one vector for each free variable, obtained by setting that variable to $1$ and the others to $0$; every basis vector must satisfy the equation.
steps: These two vectors satisfy the equation and are independent, so they form a basis.

qs.q: The general solution of the differential equation $(D+1)(D-2)^{2}(D^{2}-4D+13)y=0$ is given by
hints: Here $D=d/dx$, so the factored operator corresponds to a constant-coefficient equation whose characteristic roots can be read off.
Replace $D$ by $r$ and find all roots of the resulting polynomial, with multiplicities.
A root $r$ of multiplicity $k$ gives $e^{rx},xe^{rx},\dots,x^{k-1}e^{rx}$; roots $a\pm bi$ give $e^{ax}\cos bx,\ e^{ax}\sin bx$.
steps: Combine the five solutions with arbitrary constants.
qs.brief: Roots $-1,\ 2,\ 2,\ 2\pm3i$ give the five independent solutions listed.

qs.q: An appropriate form of a particular solution of the differential equation $y^{(3)}-y''-12y'=x-2xe^{-3x}$ is
hints: Use undetermined coefficients, and compare the trial forms with the solutions of the homogeneous equation.
Find the roots of the characteristic equation, then multiply each trial group by the smallest power of $x$ that removes any overlap with the complementary solution.
If the trial term for the right side duplicates a homogeneous solution (root $r$ of multiplicity $m$), multiply the trial form by $x^{m}$.
steps: For $x$: the basic trial $A+Bx$ overlaps with the root $r=0$, so multiply by $x$: $Ax+Bx^{2}$.
For $xe^{-3x}$: the basic trial $(C+Dx)e^{-3x}$ overlaps with root $r=-3$, so multiply by $x$: $(Cx+Dx^{2})e^{-3x}$.
qs.brief: Roots $0,4,-3$: both groups overlap, multiply each by $x$.

qs.q: If $y(x)$ is the solution of the initial-value problem $y''+4y=2x,\ y(0)=1,\ y'(0)=2$, then $y(2\pi)=$
hints: This is a nonhomogeneous constant-coefficient linear equation: complementary solution plus particular solution.
Find the complementary solution from the characteristic equation, try a polynomial for $y_p$, then use both initial conditions.
For roots $r=\pm bi$ the solutions are $\cos bx,\sin bx$; for a right side that is a polynomial of degree $n$, try a polynomial of degree $n$.

qs.q: Using variation of parameters, the differential equation $y''-2y'+y=\dfrac{e^{x}}{1+x^{2}}$ has a particular solution $y_p=u_1(x)e^{x}+u_2(x)xe^{x}$, then $u_1(x)=$
hints: This is variation of parameters with the two given solutions $y_1=e^x$, $y_2=xe^x$.
Compute the Wronskian of $y_1,y_2$ and then the formula for $u_1'$ using the right-hand side $f(x)$ of $y''+py'+qy=f$.

qs.q: The largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-3&1\\2&-1&1\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}$ is equal to
hints: Eigenvalues are roots of the characteristic equation.
Expand $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ along the third row, which has only one nonzero entry.
Eigenvalues satisfy $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$.

qs.q: If $V=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha\\1\\\beta\end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-3&1\\2&-1&1\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}$ associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda=1$, then $10\alpha+6\beta=$
hints: An eigenvector satisfies $AV=\lambda V$.
Write out $(A-I)V=\mathbf 0$ as equations in $\alpha,\beta$.
$V$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda$ exactly when $(A-\lambda I)V=\mathbf0$ and $V\neq\mathbf0$.

qs.q: An eigenvector associated with eigenvalue $\lambda=2i$ of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&8\\-1&-2\end{bmatrix}$ is
hints: Solve $(A-\lambda I)V=\mathbf0$ with a complex $\lambda$.
Write the first row of $A-2iI$ as an equation in the two components and choose a convenient value for one component.
Eigenvectors satisfy $(A-\lambda I)V=\mathbf0$; the rows of $A-\lambda I$ are dependent, so one row is enough.

qs.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\-4&7&2\\10&-15&-4\end{bmatrix}$. A basis for the eigenspace of $A$ associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ of $A$ is
hints: The eigenspace for $\lambda$ is the null space of $A-\lambda I$.
Form $A-I$ and row reduce; count the free variables.
The eigenspace is the solution set of $(A-\lambda I)V=\mathbf0$; its basis has one vector per free variable.
steps: Row 3 is $-\tfrac52$ times row 2, so the only equation is $-4x+6y+2z=0$, i.e. $z=2x-3y$.

qs.q: The roots of the indicial equation at $x=0$ for the differential equation $2xy''-y'+2y=0$ are
hints: The point $x=0$ is a regular singular point, so use the Frobenius method.
Substitute $y=x^{r}$ (leading term of the series) and keep only the lowest power of $x$.
For $x^2y''+xp(x)y'+q(x)y=0$ the indicial equation is $r(r-1)+p(0)r+q(0)=0$.

qs.q: If the general solution of the system $X'=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&1\\6&-1&0\\-1&-2&-1\end{bmatrix}X$ is given by $X=c_1\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\\-2\end{bmatrix}e^{3t}+c_2\begin{bmatrix}\alpha\\\beta\\1\end{bmatrix}e^{\lambda t}+c_3\begin{bmatrix}e\\f\\13\end{bmatrix}$, then $a\cdot b\cdot\lambda=$
hints: Each term is an eigenvalue-eigenvector solution $Ve^{\lambda t}$, so find the eigenvalues of the matrix and match the vectors.
Find the characteristic equation, then the eigenvector for $\lambda=3$ (to get $a,b$) and the eigenvalue belonging to the other vectors. Note the third term has no exponential factor.
Solutions of $X'=AX$ of the form $Ve^{\lambda t}$ need $(A-\lambda I)V=\mathbf0$; a term with no exponential factor corresponds to $\lambda=0$.
steps: The third term has no exponential factor, so it is the $\lambda=0$ eigenvector (check: $(e,f,13)=(-1,-6,13)$ satisfies $AV=\mathbf0$). Hence the second term has $\lambda=-4$.

qs.q: Let $F(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3\\-1\end{bmatrix},\ e^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}e^{t}&0\\0&e^{2t}\end{bmatrix}$. A particular solution for the system $X'=AX+F(t)$ is
hints: Use variation of parameters for systems with the fundamental matrix $e^{At}$.
Compute $e^{-At}F(t)$, integrate it with respect to $t$, and multiply by $e^{At}$.
$X_p=\Phi(t)\int\Phi(t)^{-1}F(t)\,dt$ with $\Phi=e^{At}$ and $\Phi^{-1}=e^{-At}$.

qs.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}6&4\\-9&-6\end{bmatrix}$, then $e^{At}=$
hints: Check what powers of $A$ look like; the matrix may be nilpotent.
Compute $A^2$. If it is the zero matrix, the series for $e^{At}$ stops after two terms.
$e^{At}=I+At+\dfrac{A^2t^2}{2!}+\dfrac{A^3t^3}{3!}+\cdots$
steps: So all higher powers vanish and $e^{At}=I+At$.

qs.q: A possible fundamental matrix for the system $X'=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-4&2\end{bmatrix}X$ is
hints: A fundamental matrix has linearly independent solutions as columns, so find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Solve $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ and find an eigenvector for each root.
Each eigenpair gives a solution $Ve^{\lambda t}$; put these solutions side by side as columns of $\Phi(t)$.

qs.q: If $y=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}C_nx^{n}$ is a power series solution about the ordinary point $x=0$ of the differential equation $y''-2xy'+y=0$, then the coefficients $C_n$ satisfy
hints: Substitute the power series into the equation and collect equal powers of $x$.
Differentiate the series twice, shift indices so each sum has $x^n$, and set the total coefficient of $x^n$ equal to zero.
$y'=\sum nC_nx^{n-1}$, $y''=\sum n(n-1)C_nx^{n-2}=\sum (n+2)(n+1)C_{n+2}x^n$, and $xy'=\sum nC_nx^n$.

qs.q: The minimum radius of convergence of the power series solutions for the differential equation $(x^{2}-2x+5)y''+xy'-y=0$ about the ordinary point $x=0$ is
hints: The radius is at least the distance from the expansion point to the nearest singular point in the complex plane.
Find where the coefficient of $y''$ vanishes (it can be complex) and measure its distance from $x=0$.
For $P(x)y''+Q(x)y'+R(x)y=0$, a power series solution about $x_0$ has radius of convergence at least the distance from $x_0$ to the nearest (possibly complex) zero of $P$.
steps: The minimum radius of convergence is $\sqrt5$.

qs.q: The general solution of the system $X'=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\6&-1\end{bmatrix}X$ is given by
hints: This is a constant-coefficient system, so use the eigenvalue method.
Find the eigenvalues, then an eigenvector for each, and pair each vector with its own exponential.
If $(A-\lambda I)V=\mathbf0$ then $Ve^{\lambda t}$ solves $X'=AX$; distinct real eigenvalues give a general solution $c_1V_1e^{\lambda_1t}+c_2V_2e^{\lambda_2t}$.

qs.q: If $X=c_1\begin{bmatrix}5\\-6\end{bmatrix}e^{3t}+c_2\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}e^{4t}$ is the solution of the initial value problem $X'=\begin{bmatrix}9&5\\-6&-2\end{bmatrix}X,\ X(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}$, then $c_2-c_1=$
hints: Use the initial condition at $t=0$, where the exponentials equal $1$.
Set $t=0$ in the given form of $X$ and equate components to get two equations for $c_1,c_2$.

qs.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}5&-3\\2&0\end{bmatrix}$. If $P$ is diagonalizing matrix such that $P^{-1}AP=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, then
hints: In $P^{-1}AP=D$ the columns of $P$ are eigenvectors, in the same order as the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$.
Find an eigenvector for $\lambda=2$ (first column) and for $\lambda=3$ (second column).
If $P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ then column $j$ of $P$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda_j$, i.e. $(A-\lambda_jI)V_j=\mathbf0$.

qs.q: A $2\times2$ real matrix $A$ has an eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}2+2i\\-1\end{bmatrix}$ associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda=2i$ of $A$. Then the general solution of the system $X'=AX$ is
hints: Complex eigenvalue: the real and imaginary parts of $Ve^{\lambda t}$ are two real solutions.
Multiply the eigenvector by $e^{2it}=\cos2t+i\sin2t$ and separate real and imaginary parts.

If $\lambda=a+bi$ has eigenvector $V$, then $\operatorname{Re}\left(Ve^{\lambda t}\right)$ and $\operatorname{Im}\left(Ve^{\lambda t}\right)$ are independent real solutions, and $e^{(a+bi)t}=e^{at}(\cos bt+i\sin bt)$.
qs.brief: Real and imaginary parts of $Ve^{2it}$ give the two solutions.

qs.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}5&-4\\3&-2\end{bmatrix},\ \Phi(t)=\begin{bmatrix}e^{t}&4e^{2t}\\e^{t}&3e^{2t}\end{bmatrix}$. If $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix for the system $X'=AX$, then $e^{At}=$
hints: A fundamental matrix and $e^{At}$ both solve $\Phi'=A\Phi$, so they differ by a constant matrix on the right.
Compute $\Phi(0)$ and its inverse, then multiply on the right.
$e^{At}=\Phi(t)\,\Phi(0)^{-1}$, and $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}^{-1}=\dfrac1{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$.

qs.q: The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}5&1&6\\-1&1&-3\\0&1&3\end{bmatrix}$ has a defective eigenvalue $\lambda=3$ of defect 2. Choosing $V_3=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}$ such that $(A-3I)^3V_3=0$ and $(A-3I)^2V_3\neq0$, then the general solution of the system $X'=AX$ is
hints: With a defective eigenvalue of defect 2 you need a chain of generalized eigenvectors of length 3.
Starting from $V_3$, build the chain by repeatedly multiplying by $A-3I$.
For a length-3 chain $V_3\to V_2=(A-\lambda I)V_3\to V_1=(A-\lambda I)V_2$, the solutions are $V_1e^{\lambda t}$, $(V_2+tV_1)e^{\lambda t}$, $\left(V_3+tV_2+\tfrac{t^2}{2}V_1\right)e^{\lambda t}$.
